newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK inflation rise spells government setback.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK inflation rise spells government setback.

text.p: Britain's underlying rate of inflation rose to an annual 2.9 percent in September, a setback that will make it more difficult for the ruling Conservatives to justify pre-election cuts in taxes and interest rates.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said headline inflation was steady at 2.1 percent, but the underlying rate, which excludes mortgage interest payments, edged up from 2.8 percent where it had been stuck for four months.
"The major upward effects on the 12-month rate came from motoring costs, clothing and footwear prices and from household services' prices," the ONS said.
Clothing and footwear jumped a dramatic 5.2 percent in price in September compared with August, the largest monthly rise since records began in 1947.

The figures were bad news for the government, coming just before Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke was due to address the last Conservative Party conference before national elections that must be called by next May.

Clarke has hailed the reduction in inflation as one of the key successes of Conservative economic policy, but the September figures show underlying inflation moving away from his target of 2.5 percent.
Nevertheless, the Chancellor was undaunted. "I believe we are absolutely in line to meet the inflation target," he told Reuters in Bournemouth.
The Treasury insisted cost pressures in the economy remained subdued, while Clarke said the "feelgood factor" was returning and predicted this would win the election for the government.

However, September price data are the basis on which state social security benefits and pensions will be increased next year, so they will lead to increased public spending, making it harder for Clarke to justify tax cuts in his November 26 budget.

Higher inflation also undermines the Chancellor's case for another cut in interest rates, which would be welcomed by millions of home-owners. "This figure will be a double blow for Clarke," said Alex Garrard, an economist at stockbrokers UBS, who estimated that the pickup in inflation could add as much as 500 million pounds ($781.9 million) to government spending on pensions and social security.
"It's a further headache for Clarke's budget sums and cramps his scope for tax cuts."
City economists said retailers appeared to have taken advantage of rising turnover to increase profit margins that had been battered by recession earlier in the 1990s.
But Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets, said it was too early to say that a high street spending spree would fuel retail price inflation.
"Consumers are still looking for value for money in the high street and the steep drop in factory gate inflation should soon start to feed through into core retail price inflation."
The pickup in inflation will add fuel to the Bank of England's call for a rise in interest rates.
The central bank, worried that inflation may be set for a resurgence by mid-1998, has been calling since July for official rates to be raised to 6.0 percent from the present 5.75 percent.

But Clarke, who as finance minister has the final say on monetary policy, has rejected its advice and economists said it was highly unlikely he would agree to put up interest rates ahead of an election.
